items.title: Winard Harper interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, October 10, 2014
items.q: When you go back and you listen to Duke Ellington, Louis Armstrong, Charlie Parker, John Coltrane

ctx.x: My daughter actually plays in an African drum ensemble in Rochester. And I go to see them. It’s led by a fellow from West Africa. And it would annoy me — the music was incredible but I would get annoyed when I couldn’t put — where’s 1? You know, I’d lose it. And I don’t think I should be annoyed but I kept trying to codify it into something I could feel like I understood.

Yeah, for them it’s there. It’s just like, you know, they have whatever that clave is, that gets held down, because one of those instruments usually is holding everything down, where you can say okay — but then all of them polyrhythms go on top. And that’s where you start to hear all these other voices. But there’s something nailing it, holding it down. But it’s so interesting. And that’s what jazz, how jazz evolved, out of that. Jazz is still a language. It’s speaking. It should be saying something. And…
You know it was that, it was a part of that, but there was still some other very meaningful —
